## [Homepage](../index.html)

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| echo: false

#| purl: false

knitr::purl("un_E.qmd", output = "../code/un_E.R", documentation = 0)
styler:::style_file("../code/un_E.R")

library(ggplot2)
library(ggthemes)
library(MLGdata)
```

- In [Unit C](un_C.html) and [Unit D](un_D.html) we saw that binomial and Poisson regression may suffer from [overdispersion]{.orange}: the data are more variable than the model allows.

- This unit presents [quasi-likelihoods]{.blue} [@Wedderburn1974], a simple way to handle overdispersion [without]{.orange} specifying a distribution for $Y_i$: we only specify its [mean]{.blue} and its [variance]{.orange}.

- The unit is organized in three parts:
  - a [motivating example]{.blue}, the `Ants` data;
  - the [theory]{.orange} of quasi-likelihood models;
  - the [complete analysis]{.grey} of the example.

- An alternative, [not covered]{.grey} in this course, is to replace the Poisson or the binomial with a different parametric distribution, e.g. the negative binomial.

:::callout-tip
The content of this Unit is covered in [Chapter 6]{.orange} of @Salvan2020. Alternatively, see [Sections 8.1 and 8.3]{.blue} of @Agresti2015.
:::

```{r}
#| label: setup-models
#| include: false
# Data preparation and all the fitted models used in this unit
data(Ants)
Ants$Bread <- as.factor(Ants$Bread)
Ants$Filling <- as.factor(Ants$Filling)
Ants$Butter <- as.factor(Ants$Butter)

pv <- function(p) ifelse(p < 0.001, "<0.001", sprintf("%.3f", p))

# Poisson model
m_pois <- glm(Ant_count ~ Bread + Filling * Butter, family = poisson, data = Ants)
cf_pois <- summary(m_pois)$coefficients
X2 <- sum(residuals(m_pois, type = "pearson")^2)
X2_pvalue <- pchisq(X2, df = m_pois$df.residual, lower.tail = FALSE)

# Quasi-Poisson model
m_quasi <- glm(Ant_count ~ Bread + Filling * Butter,
  family = quasi(link = "log", variance = "mu"), data = Ants
)
cf_quasi <- summary(m_quasi)$coefficients
phi_hat <- summary(m_quasi)$dispersion

# Model simplification
d1 <- drop1(m_quasi, test = "Chisq")
m_quasi1 <- update(m_quasi, . ~ . - Bread)
d2 <- drop1(m_quasi1, test = "Chisq")

# Final model
m_final <- update(m_quasi1, . ~ . - Filling:Butter)
cf_final <- summary(m_final)$coefficients
phi_final <- summary(m_final)$dispersion
rel_change <- round(100 * (exp(coef(m_final)) - 1))

# Confidence and prediction intervals
newdata <- data.frame(Filling = "3", Butter = "1")
pred <- predict(m_final, newdata = newdata, type = "link", se.fit = TRUE)
mu_new <- exp(pred$fit)
ci_mean <- exp(pred$fit + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(0.975) * pred$se.fit)
pi_quasi <- qnorm(c(0.025, 0.975), mean = mu_new, sd = sqrt(phi_final * mu_new))
pi_pois <- qpois(c(0.025, 0.975), lambda = mu_new)

# Simulated data without overdispersion
set.seed(123)
x_sim <- rbinom(2000, size = 1, prob = 0.5)
y_sim <- rpois(2000, lambda = exp(1 + 3 * x_sim))
m_sim <- glm(y_sim ~ x_sim, family = poisson)
phi_sim <- sum(residuals(m_sim, type = "pearson")^2) / m_sim$df.residual
```

# A motivating example

## The `Ants` data

- The `Ants` dataset of the `MLGdata` library comes from an experiment run by students of an Australian university [@Salvan2020]. The aim is to study which sandwiches [meat ants]{.orange} prefer.

- The [explanatory variables]{.blue} are three experimental factors:

  - `Bread` ($4$ types): rye, wholemeal, multigrain, white;
  - `Filling` ($3$ types): Vegemite, peanut butter, ham and pickles;
  - `Butter` ($2$ levels): present ($1$) or absent ($-1$).

- For each of the $4 \times 3 \times 2 = 24$ combinations, [two]{.orange} pieces of sandwich were placed near the entrance of an ant nest, for a total of $n = 48$ observations.

- The [response]{.blue} `Ant_count` is the number of ants on the sandwich after $5$ minutes.

## Exploratory analysis

```{r}
#| label: fig-boxplots
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-align: center
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
boxplot(Ant_count ~ Bread, data = Ants, col = "grey85")
boxplot(Ant_count ~ Filling, data = Ants, col = "grey85")
boxplot(Ant_count ~ Butter, data = Ants, col = "grey85")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

- `Filling` and `Butter` seem to matter, whereas `Bread` has a weaker effect.

- The response is a [count]{.blue}, therefore a natural starting point is a [Poisson regression]{.orange} model with logarithmic link, including the `Filling`-`Butter` interaction ($p = 9$).

## A Poisson regression model

::: {.small-table}

```{r}
#| label: tab-poisson
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Estimate = cf_pois[, 1], `Std. Error` = cf_pois[, 2], `p-value` = pv(cf_pois[, 4]),
    check.names = FALSE
  ),
  digits = 3
)
```

:::

- According to the Wald tests, `Bread2`, `Filling3` and both [interaction]{.orange} terms are significant at the $5\%$ level.

- But can we trust these standard errors?

## Is there overdispersion?

- The residual deviance is $D(\bm{y}; \hat{\bm{\mu}}) =$ `r round(deviance(m_pois), 2)` and the [Pearson statistic]{.blue} of [Unit B](un_B.html) is $X^2 =$ `r round(X2, 2)`, both on $n - p = 39$ degrees of freedom. The p-value of the $X^2$ test is `r pv(X2_pvalue)`.

- Both statistics are [more than four times]{.orange} the degrees of freedom: the data are [much more variable]{.orange} than implied by the Poisson model, in which $\text{var}(Y_i) = \mu_i$.

- The Poisson model is [misspecified]{.orange} and its standard errors are [too small]{.orange}: the significant coefficients of the previous slide should not be trusted.

:::callout-warning
A large $X^2$ may also be caused by a [misspecified mean]{.orange}, e.g. an omitted covariate, a missing interaction or a wrong link function. Correcting the standard errors is appropriate [only if]{.blue} the mean structure $g(\mu_i) = \bm{x}_i^T\beta$ is correct.
:::

## A word of caution

- A tempting shortcut is to compare the sample mean and variance of the response. In the `Ants` data they are `r round(mean(Ants$Ant_count), 1)` and `r round(var(Ants$Ant_count))`. Is this enough to conclude that there is overdispersion? [No]{.orange}.

- The Poisson assumption concerns $Y_i$ [given the covariates]{.blue}. Consider $n = 2000$ observations from
$$
Y_i \overset{\text{ind}}{\sim} \text{Poisson}(\mu_i), \qquad \log{\mu_i} = 1 + 3 x_i, \qquad x_i \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \text{Bernoulli}(0.5),
$$
which have [no overdispersion]{.orange} by construction.

- The simulated data have mean `r round(mean(y_sim), 1)` and variance `r round(var(y_sim), 1)`, simply because the covariate shifts the mean. Once the covariate is accounted for, the Poisson fit gives $X^2/(n-p) =$ `r round(phi_sim, 3)`.

:::callout-tip
Back to the `Ants` data: how can we fix the standard errors, [without]{.orange} having to choose a new distribution for the counts?
:::

# Quasi-likelihoods

## A motivating remark: the linear model

- In the [Gaussian linear model]{.blue} $\bm{Y} = \bm{X}\beta + \bm{\epsilon}$ with $\epsilon_i \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \text{N}(0, \sigma^2)$, the maximum likelihood estimator $\hat{\beta} = (\bm{X}^T\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^T\bm{y}$ has the [exact]{.blue} distribution
$$
\hat{\beta} \sim \text{N}_p(\beta, \sigma^2(\bm{X}^T\bm{X})^{-1}).
$$

- In [Unit A](un_A.html) we saw that under the much weaker [second-order assumptions]{.orange} $\mathbb{E}(\bm{\epsilon}) = \bm{0}$ and $\text{var}(\bm{\epsilon}) = \sigma^2 I_n$, the same estimator is still [unbiased]{.blue}, with $\text{var}(\hat{\beta}) = \sigma^2(\bm{X}^T\bm{X})^{-1}$, and [asymptotically normal]{.blue}.

:::callout-tip
If the normal model is misspecified but the second-order assumptions hold, the inference based on the normal model remains [valid for large $n$]{.orange}. Gaussianity is only needed for [exact]{.blue} results.
:::

- [Question]{.blue}: does the same happen for the maximum likelihood estimator of a [GLM]{.orange}?

## Likelihood equations of a GLM

- Let $Y_i \overset{\text{ind}}{\sim} \text{ED}(\mu_i, a_i(\phi)v(\mu_i))$ with $g(\mu_i) = \bm{x}_i^T\beta$ and $a_i(\phi) = \phi/\omega_i$. Recall from [Unit B](un_B.html) that the [likelihood equations]{.blue} are
$$
\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{(y_i - \mu_i)}{\text{var}(Y_i)}\frac{\partial \mu_i}{\partial \beta_r} = \frac{1}{\phi}\sum_{i=1}^n \omega_i\frac{(y_i - \mu_i)}{v(\mu_i)}\frac{x_{ir}}{g'(\mu_i)} = 0, \qquad r=1,\dots,p.
$$

- These equations depend on the distribution of $Y_i$ [only]{.orange} through
$$
\mathbb{E}(Y_i) = \mu_i = g^{-1}(\bm{x}_i^T\beta), \qquad \text{var}(Y_i) = \frac{\phi}{\omega_i}v(\mu_i).
$$

- Higher-order moments, such as the skewness, have [no impact]{.orange} on the equations: any distribution with the same first two moments leads to the [same]{.blue} estimate $\hat{\beta}$. They only affect the [distribution]{.grey} of $\hat{\beta}$, e.g. how quickly it approaches normality.

## The quasi-likelihood model

:::callout-note
The [quasi-likelihood model]{.blue} only assumes the following [second-order]{.orange} conditions:

- **(E.1)** $\quad\mathbb{E}(Y_i) = \mu_i = g^{-1}(\bm{x}_i^T\beta)$;

- **(E.2)** $\quad\text{var}(Y_i) = \dfrac{\phi}{\omega_i}v(\mu_i)$, with $\phi > 0$ [unknown]{.orange};

- **(E.3)** $\quad Y_i$ and $Y_j$ are independent for $i \neq j$.
:::

- This is a [semiparametric]{.blue} model: only the first two moments of $Y_i$ are specified.

- The estimate $\hat{\beta}$ is defined as the solution of the [estimating equations]{.blue}
$$
\sum_{i=1}^n \omega_i\frac{(y_i - \mu_i)}{v(\mu_i)}\frac{x_{ir}}{g'(\mu_i)} = 0, \qquad r=1,\dots,p,
$$
which do not depend on $\phi$ and can be solved with the [IRLS]{.orange} algorithm of [Unit B](un_B.html), [whatever]{.orange} the choice of $v(\cdot)$.

## Variance inflation

- For the [Gaussian]{.grey} model, **(E.2)** is the usual homoscedasticity assumption, with $\phi = \sigma^2$. The novelty concerns [counts]{.blue} and [proportions]{.blue}, for which the GLM imposes $\phi = 1$.

- Keeping the variance function of a GLM, **(E.2)** [inflates]{.orange} its variance by the factor $\phi$. We have [overdispersion]{.orange} if $\phi > 1$ and [underdispersion]{.blue} if $\phi < 1$, which is far less common.

- The two most common quasi-likelihood models are:
  - the [quasi-Poisson]{.blue} model, with $\text{var}(Y_i) = \phi\,\mu_i$;
  - the [quasi-binomial]{.orange} model, with $\text{var}(Y_i) = \phi\,\mu_i(1-\mu_i)/m_i$.

- In both cases the estimating equations are the likelihood equations of the Poisson or binomial GLM, hence $\hat{\beta}$ is the [maximum likelihood estimate]{.blue} of the GLM.

:::callout-warning
As noted in [Unit C](un_C.html), the quasi-binomial model makes sense only for [grouped]{.orange} data. With binary data ($m_i = 1$) we necessarily have $\text{var}(Y_i) = \mu_i(1-\mu_i)$, hence $\phi = 1$.
:::

## Where does overdispersion come from?

- [Unobserved heterogeneity]{.blue}. Units with the same covariates may differ because of unrecorded variables. If $Y_i \mid U_i \sim \text{Poisson}(U_i\mu_i)$, with $\mathbb{E}(U_i) = 1$ and $\text{var}(U_i) = \sigma^2$, then
$$
\mathbb{E}(Y_i) = \mu_i, \qquad \text{var}(Y_i) = \mathbb{E}\{\text{var}(Y_i \mid U_i)\} + \text{var}\{\mathbb{E}(Y_i \mid U_i)\} = \mu_i + \sigma^2\mu_i^2.
$$

- [Correlated trials]{.orange}. Let $S_i = m_i Y_i = \sum_{j=1}^{m_i} Z_{ij}$, with $Z_{ij} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\mu_i)$ having correlation $\rho > 0$, e.g. fetuses of the same litter. Then
$$
\text{var}(Y_i) = \frac{\mu_i(1-\mu_i)}{m_i}\{1 + \rho(m_i - 1)\}.
$$

- In both cases the inflation factor is [not constant]{.orange}: variance inflation is only an [approximation]{.blue}.

:::callout-tip
Other variance functions are possible, e.g. $v(\mu) = \mu^2$ for counts, or $v(\mu) = \mu^2(1-\mu)^2$ for proportions [@Wedderburn1974], which corresponds to [no likelihood]{.orange}. A different $v(\cdot)$ also changes the estimate.
:::

## The quasi-score

- The left-hand side of the estimating equations, divided by $\phi$, is called [quasi-score]{.blue}:
$$
q_r(\beta) = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{(Y_i - \mu_i)}{\text{var}(Y_i)}\frac{\partial \mu_i}{\partial \beta_r}, \qquad r = 1,\dots,p.
$$

- Under **(E.1)**-**(E.3)** alone, the quasi-score satisfies the [Bartlett identities]{.orange} of a genuine score function, that is $\mathbb{E}\{q_r(\beta)\} = 0$ and
$$
\mathbb{E}\{q_r(\beta)q_s(\beta)\} = -\mathbb{E}\left\{\frac{\partial q_r(\beta)}{\partial \beta_s}\right\} = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{\text{var}(Y_i)}\frac{\partial \mu_i}{\partial \beta_r}\frac{\partial \mu_i}{\partial \beta_s} = [\bm{X}^T\bm{W}\bm{X}]_{rs},
$$
where $\bm{W} = \text{diag}(w_1,\dots,w_n)$ are the weights of [Unit B](un_B.html).

:::callout-tip
The quasi-score behaves like a genuine score, even though no distribution has been specified. This explains the name [quasi-likelihood]{.blue}, and it is the key to the asymptotic results.
:::

## Properties of $\hat{\beta}$

:::callout-warning
Under the assumptions **(E.1)**-**(E.3)**, the estimator $\hat{\beta}$ is [consistent]{.blue} and [asymptotically normal]{.orange}:
$$
\hat{\beta} \: \dot{\sim} \: \text{N}_p\left(\beta, (\bm{X}^T\bm{W}\bm{X})^{-1}\right), \qquad w_i = \frac{1}{\text{var}(Y_i)g'(\mu_i)^2} = \frac{1}{\phi}\frac{\omega_i}{v(\mu_i) g'(\mu_i)^2}.
$$
:::

- This is [formally identical]{.orange} to the result of [Unit B](un_B.html), but it now holds under much [weaker assumptions]{.blue}.

- Does it make sense to talk about the [exact]{.blue} distribution of $\hat{\beta}$? [No]{.orange}: it would require the distribution of $Y_i$, which we deliberately left unspecified.

- Consistency only requires **(E.1)**: if the [mean]{.blue} is correctly specified, $\hat{\beta}$ is consistent even when $v(\mu_i)$ is wrong. The [standard errors]{.orange}, however, rely on **(E.2)**.

## Estimation of $\phi$ and standard errors

- The dispersion $\phi$ is estimated with the [method of moments]{.blue} estimator of [Unit B](un_B.html), which is [consistent]{.orange} under **(E.1)**-**(E.3)**:
$$
\hat{\phi} = \frac{X^2}{n - p} = \frac{1}{n - p}\sum_{i=1}^n \omega_i \frac{(y_i - \hat{\mu}_i)^2}{v(\hat{\mu}_i)}.
$$

- The standard errors are obtained from $(\bm{X}^T\hat{\bm{W}}\bm{X})^{-1}$, plugging in $\hat{\beta}$ and $\hat{\phi}$. The weights $w_i$ are [inversely proportional]{.orange} to $\phi$.

:::callout-note
#### Variance inflation in a nutshell

When $v(\cdot)$ is the variance function of a GLM, as in the quasi-Poisson and quasi-binomial models:

1. Fit the [ordinary GLM]{.blue} and keep its maximum likelihood estimate $\hat{\beta}$.

2. Multiply the [standard errors]{.orange} of the GLM by $\sqrt{\hat{\phi}}$, that is $[\widehat{\text{se}}_\text{quasi}(\hat{\beta})]_j = \sqrt{\hat{\phi}}\,[\widehat{\text{se}}_\text{glm}(\hat{\beta})]_j$.
:::

## The quasi-log-likelihood

- To compare nested models we need something like a log-likelihood. Under **(E.1)**-**(E.3)** we define the [quasi-log-likelihood]{.blue}
$$
\ell_Q(\beta, \phi) = \sum_{i=1}^n \int_{y_i}^{\mu_i} \frac{\omega_i(y_i - t)}{\phi\,v(t)}\,\mathrm{d}t, \qquad \mu_i = g^{-1}(\bm{x}_i^T\beta).
$$

- Its derivatives are the [quasi-score]{.orange} $q_r(\beta)$. Indeed, if $F(\cdot)$ is a primitive of $t \mapsto \omega_i(y_i - t)/\{\phi\,v(t)\}$, then
$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_r}\{F(\mu_i) - F(y_i)\} = F'(\mu_i)\frac{\partial \mu_i}{\partial \beta_r} = \frac{(y_i - \mu_i)}{\text{var}(Y_i)}\frac{\partial \mu_i}{\partial \beta_r}.
$$

- In general $\ell_Q(\beta, \phi)$ is [not]{.orange} a log-likelihood. However, in the Poisson case ($\omega_i = 1$, $v(t) = t$, $\phi = 1$) we get $\ell_Q(\beta, 1) = \sum_{i=1}^n(y_i \log{\mu_i} - \mu_i)$, up to constants, which is the [Poisson log-likelihood]{.blue}.

## Comparing nested models

- The quantity $D(\bm{y}; \bm{\mu}) = -2\phi\,\ell_Q(\beta, \phi)$ is called [quasi-deviance]{.blue}. When $v(\cdot)$ is the variance function of a GLM, it coincides with the [deviance]{.orange} of [Unit B](un_B.html), e.g. the Poisson or the binomial one.

- Let $M_0 \subset M_1$ be two [nested models]{.grey}, with $p_0$ and $p$ parameters, and let $q = p - p_0$. The [quasi-log-likelihood ratio]{.blue} statistic is
$$
W = 2[\ell_Q(\hat{\beta}, \hat{\phi}) - \ell_Q(\hat{\beta}_0, \hat{\phi})] = \frac{D(\bm{y}; \hat{\bm{\mu}}_0) - D(\bm{y}; \hat{\bm{\mu}})}{\hat{\phi}} \: \dot{\sim} \: \chi^2_q,
$$
where $\hat{\phi}$ is estimated from the [larger]{.orange} model.

:::callout-warning
- The (quasi-)deviances must [not]{.orange} be used as goodness-of-fit statistics, since $\phi$ is unknown.

- There is no likelihood, therefore the [AIC]{.orange} is [not available]{.orange}.
:::

# The `Ants` data

## The quasi-Poisson model

- With the same mean structure, we obtain $\hat{\phi} =$ `r round(phi_hat, 2)`: the standard errors are multiplied by $\sqrt{\hat{\phi}} =$ `r round(sqrt(phi_hat), 2)`.

::: {.small-table}

```{r}
#| label: tab-quasi
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Estimate = cf_quasi[, 1],
    `SE (Poisson)` = cf_pois[, 2], `SE (quasi)` = cf_quasi[, 2],
    `p-value (Poisson)` = pv(cf_pois[, 4]), `p-value (quasi)` = pv(cf_quasi[, 4]),
    check.names = FALSE
  ),
  digits = 3
)
```

:::

- The [estimates]{.blue} are identical. After the correction, only `Filling3` remains [significant]{.orange}.

## Model simplification

- The larger standard errors suggest a [simpler]{.blue} model. We remove one term at a time, using the quasi-log-likelihood ratio statistic $W$ and its $\chi^2_q$ approximation.

```{r}
#| label: tab-simplification
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Model = c("Full model", "Full model", "Without Bread"),
    `Removed term` = c("Bread", "Filling:Butter", "Filling:Butter"),
    q = c(d1["Bread", "Df"], d1["Filling:Butter", "Df"], d2["Filling:Butter", "Df"]),
    W = c(d1["Bread", "scaled dev."], d1["Filling:Butter", "scaled dev."], d2["Filling:Butter", "scaled dev."]),
    `p-value` = pv(c(d1["Bread", "Pr(>Chi)"], d1["Filling:Butter", "Pr(>Chi)"], d2["Filling:Butter", "Pr(>Chi)"])),
    check.names = FALSE
  ),
  digits = 3
)
```

- Neither `Bread` nor the `Filling`-`Butter` interaction are relevant, once overdispersion is accounted for.

- The final model only includes `Filling` and `Butter`, with $p = 4$ parameters.

## The final model

```{r}
#| label: tab-final
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Estimate = cf_final[, 1], `Std. Error` = cf_final[, 2], `p-value` = pv(cf_final[, 4]),
    `exp(Estimate)` = exp(cf_final[, 1]),
    check.names = FALSE
  ),
  digits = 3
)
```

- Under the logarithmic link, $\exp(\beta_j)$ is the [multiplicative change]{.blue} of the mean number of ants ([Unit D](un_D.html)). The estimated dispersion is $\hat{\phi} =$ `r round(phi_final, 2)`.

- Compared to Vegemite, [ham and pickles]{.orange} attract on average about `r rel_change["Filling3"]`% more ants, and peanut butter about `r rel_change["Filling2"]`% more (borderline significant).

- The presence of [butter]{.blue} increases the mean number of ants by about `r rel_change["Butter1"]`%. The type of bread is irrelevant.

## Confidence and prediction intervals

- Consider a sandwich with ham and pickles and butter, whose estimated mean is $\hat{\mu}_\text{new} =$ `r round(mu_new, 1)` ants. The $95\%$ intervals are:

```{r}
#| label: tab-intervals
intervals <- rbind(ci_mean, pi_quasi, pi_pois)
colnames(intervals) <- c("Lower", "Upper")
rownames(intervals) <- c("Confidence interval for the mean", "Prediction interval (quasi-Poisson)", "Prediction interval (Poisson)")
knitr::kable(intervals, digits = 1)
```

- The [confidence interval]{.blue} for $\mu$ is obtained on the linear predictor scale and then transformed.

- Without a distribution, the [prediction interval]{.orange} relies on the approximation $Y_\text{new} \: \dot{\sim} \: \text{N}(\hat{\mu}_\text{new}, \hat{\phi}\hat{\mu}_\text{new})$.

- The Poisson prediction interval, based on the Poisson quantiles, is [far too narrow]{.orange}.

## Summary

- A [quasi-likelihood model]{.blue} only specifies the mean $g(\mu_i) = \bm{x}_i^T\beta$ and the variance $\text{var}(Y_i) = (\phi/\omega_i)v(\mu_i)$ of independent responses.

- The estimate $\hat{\beta}$ solves the quasi-score equations via IRLS, and it is consistent and asymptotically normal under these weaker assumptions.

- The dispersion is estimated by $\hat{\phi} = X^2/(n-p)$. In the quasi-Poisson and quasi-binomial models, $\hat{\beta}$ is the GLM estimate and [all]{.orange} standard errors are multiplied by $\sqrt{\hat{\phi}}$.

- Nested models are compared through the difference of deviances divided by $\hat{\phi}$. The AIC is not available.

- In practice, overdispersion is [very common]{.orange} with counts and grouped proportions. Ignoring it leads to [overconfident]{.orange} conclusions, as in the `Ants` data.

## References
